body:
What is traditional knowledge?

Traditional knowledge (TK) consists of knowledge, skills, practices and innovations developed and maintained by communities over generations. It may concern agriculture, medicinal plants, food preservation, biodiversity, natural resource management or traditional methods of production.

Traditional knowledge is not necessarily ancient or unchanging. Communities may improve their practices through observation and experience. Its defining feature is its connection with the knowledge traditions of a community, rather than its age alone.

For example, a community may know which locally available plants have traditionally been used for particular purposes, when they are collected and how their use is understood within the community. Such knowledge may be transmitted orally or recorded in manuscripts and other documents.

Traditional knowledge: Knowledge, know-how, skills and practices developed, sustained and transmitted within a community, often forming part of its cultural identity and livelihood.

Traditional knowledge and biological resources

A biological resource is the biological material being used, such as a plant, microorganism or a relevant biological component. Traditional knowledge associated with a biological resource is the community's knowledge about that resource, such as a customary medicinal or agricultural use.

These are related but different things. A medicinal plant is a biological resource; knowledge of its traditional application is associated traditional knowledge. The existence of a plant does not automatically establish who discovered a particular use, and knowledge of a plant does not automatically create a patent.

The distinction matters because different legal questions arise when a researcher obtains biological material, learns about its traditional use and develops a commercial product.

ConceptMeaningExample
Biological resourceBiological material or its relevant componentsA medicinal plant collected for research
Associated traditional knowledgeCommunity knowledge concerning a resourceA traditionally known use of that plant
New inventionA claimed technical solution that must satisfy patent lawA genuinely new qualifying process developed through research
Traditional cultural expressionA form of cultural creativity or expressionA customary textile design or folk art

Traditional cultural expressions and traditional knowledge can overlap, but they should not be treated as identical. For example, Gujarat's Patola weaving traditions and distinctive Kutchi embroidery illustrate the transmission of community skills and cultural expressions. Their protection does not automatically follow the rules governing access to medicinal plants or other biological resources.

What is biopiracy?

Biopiracy generally refers to the unauthorized or unfair appropriation or commercial exploitation of biological resources or associated traditional knowledge, particularly without appropriate recognition, permission or benefit sharing.

Biopiracy may involve obtaining biological material without the required authorization, commercially exploiting community knowledge without appropriate benefit sharing, or obtaining an unjustified patent over a use that was already known.

These situations are related but are not legally identical. A patent may be wrongly granted because an alleged invention lacks novelty. Separately, access to a resource or its associated knowledge may violate biodiversity legislation or applicable agreements even when the resulting invention is genuinely new.

Why traditional knowledge is vulnerable

  • Oral transmission: Knowledge may be widely used within a community without appearing in documents searched by patent examiners.
  • Language barriers: Knowledge recorded in local languages may be overlooked during patent examination.
  • Collective development: Knowledge may belong to a long community tradition rather than one identifiable inventor.
  • Commercial imbalance: A company may have greater resources to develop and market a product than the community that supplied the original knowledge.

Protecting traditional knowledge therefore has 2 connected objectives: preventing unjustified exclusive rights over existing knowledge and ensuring fair treatment when biological resources or associated knowledge are accessed and used.

Prelims focus

  • Traditional knowledge may be medicinal, agricultural, ecological or technical.
  • It can be transmitted orally or through written records.
  • A biological resource and knowledge associated with it are different concepts.
  • Biopiracy can concern unauthorized access, unfair exploitation or unjustified intellectual property claims.
  • Trap: Every commercial use of a biological resource is not automatically biopiracy; the applicable permissions, legal conditions and benefit-sharing obligations matter.

[WIPO, Traditional Knowledge, sections 'Traditional Knowledge' and 'Traditional Knowledge and Intellectual Property', consulted 14 November 2026; NCERT, Biology, Class 12, chapter 12, 'Biotechnology and Its Applications', section 12.4; NCERT, Living Craft Traditions of India, Class 11, 'Crafts Heritage', printed pp. 9–14; NCERT, Science, Class 8, chapter 7, 'Conservation of Plants and Animals'.]

title: Traditional Knowledge, Biological Resources and the Meaning of Biopiracy

body:
Why documentation matters

Patent law is intended to protect qualifying inventions, not grant exclusive rights over knowledge that was already available. To assess whether an invention is new, patent examiners examine prior art: relevant information made available before the applicable patent filing or priority date.

Prior art may include earlier patents, scientific publications, books and other publicly available disclosures. Traditional practices can also be relevant. The difficulty is establishing what was previously known and presenting reliable evidence of it in a form that patent examiners can examine.

For example, suppose a patent application claims the already documented traditional use of turmeric for wound healing. Evidence that this use was known before the application can establish that the claimed subject matter is not new. The fact that the earlier knowledge was recorded in an Indian language does not make it a new invention in another country.

Prior art answers a patentability question: Was the claimed invention already known or disclosed before the relevant date? It does not, by itself, determine whether a user obtained biological resources lawfully or shared benefits fairly.

How traditional knowledge can be documented

Documentation may involve recording local names of resources, their characteristics, customary uses, relevant community knowledge and the source of that information. Written descriptions, historical publications and appropriately maintained community records can help preserve and establish knowledge.

However, documentation does not automatically create ownership or an exclusive intellectual property right. A record may preserve evidence, support conservation or help oppose an unjustified patent without giving its compiler a patent over the recorded knowledge.

Documentation also creates a risk when knowledge was previously confidential or restricted within a community. Making such information freely accessible may expose it to unwanted commercial use. Communities therefore need appropriate consent, safeguards and decisions about which information should be recorded or disclosed.

India's Traditional Knowledge Digital Library

The Traditional Knowledge Digital Library (TKDL) is an Indian initiative developed by the Council of Scientific and Industrial Research (CSIR) and the Government of India's Department of Indian Systems of Medicine and Homoeopathy (now the Ministry of Ayush). The initiative began in 2001 to address the problem of patents being granted over previously documented Indian traditional medicinal knowledge.

Many Indian medicinal formulations were described in Sanskrit and other languages unfamiliar to overseas patent examiners. An examiner searching only conventional patent databases could therefore overlook relevant traditional knowledge.

TKDL makes the content of existing published traditional medicinal texts searchable and understandable for patent examination. It covers documented knowledge from Ayurveda, Unani, Siddha, Sowa Rigpa and Yoga.

It uses the Traditional Knowledge Resource Classification (TKRC) to classify information and provide access in 5 international languages: English, French, German, Japanese and Spanish.

Who uses TKDL?

Authorized patent offices receive access under agreements that restrict disclosure and use of the database. Examiners can compare patent claims with recorded traditional knowledge and use relevant prior-art evidence when examining applications.

TKDL is therefore mainly a defensive intellectual property measure. It helps prevent wrongful patent grants. It does not give CSIR ownership of every medicinal practice recorded in the database, nor does it automatically establish a benefit-sharing arrangement for every community.

Defensive and positive protection

ProtectionMain objectiveIllustrative method
Defensive protectionPrevent outsiders from obtaining unjustified exclusive rights over existing knowledgePrior-art documentation, patent examination and opposition
Positive protectionEnable knowledge-holders to control or benefit from permitted usesApplicable community rights, agreements, benefit sharing and suitable IP mechanisms

Positive protection may involve agreements specifying permitted uses, recognition of community interests and sharing benefits arising from commercial utilization. Existing legal mechanisms such as geographical indications, confidentiality arrangements and biodiversity law may be relevant in particular circumstances. No single mechanism protects every kind of traditional knowledge.

The strongest approach often combines careful documentation with legal safeguards. Documentation can help demonstrate what was already known, while consent and benefit-sharing arrangements address whether and how the knowledge may be used.

Prelims focus

  • Prior art: Relevant knowledge or disclosure existing before the applicable patent date.
  • TKDL: Traditional Knowledge Digital Library, initiated in 2001.
  • Institution: CSIR is a principal institution behind TKDL.
  • TKRC: Traditional Knowledge Resource Classification.
  • TKDL supports patent examination through evidence of existing traditional medicinal knowledge.
  • Trap: Documentation and defensive protection do not automatically grant a patent or establish community ownership.

[CSIR, Traditional Knowledge Digital Library Unit, sections 'About TKDL' and 'TKDL Journey', consulted 14 November 2026; CSIR-TKDL, 'Bio-piracy of Traditional Knowledge', sections 'Protecting Codified Traditional Knowledge' and 'TKDL', consulted 14 November 2026; WIPO, Traditional Knowledge, sections 'Defensive Protection' and 'Positive Protection', consulted 14 November 2026; WIPO, Traditional Knowledge Documentation Toolkit, documentation and safeguarding guidance, consulted 14 November 2026.]

title: Documenting Traditional Knowledge: Prior Art, TKDL and Protection Strategies

body:
Why these disputes are important

Three widely discussed intellectual property disputes involving turmeric, neem and Basmati rice illustrate how claims based on traditional uses or biological resources can be challenged. They also demonstrate why it is necessary to distinguish a patent on a specific claimed invention from ownership of an entire plant, crop or traditional practice.

Turmeric: a traditional medicinal use and novelty

Turmeric has long been used in Indian traditional practices, including applications associated with wound healing. In 1995, a United States patent, US 5,401,504, was granted for the use of turmeric in wound healing.

CSIR challenged the patent through a re-examination request before the United States Patent and Trademark Office. It presented evidence of earlier knowledge, including published material documenting turmeric's traditional wound-healing use.

The patent was cancelled in 1997 because the claimed use lacked the required novelty in light of existing knowledge.

The central lesson is that a known application does not become a new invention merely because it is described in modern patent language or claimed in another country.

Neem: evidence of an existing agricultural application

Neem has traditionally been used in India for several purposes, including agricultural applications. A European patent concerning the use of a particular neem-oil preparation to control fungi on plants was granted in 1994.

Opponents, including organizations representing environmental and farming interests, challenged the patent by relying on evidence of earlier knowledge and use of neem-based preparations.

The European Patent Office revoked the patent in May 2000. The dispute involved whether the claimed invention met patentability requirements, including inventive step, in view of the existing evidence.

It is inaccurate to describe this as a patent granting ownership of the neem tree itself. The dispute concerned particular patent claims relating to a neem-based application.

Basmati: existing rice varieties and the limits of a patent claim

Basmati rice has a long history of cultivation in the Indian subcontinent. In 1997, the United States Patent and Trademark Office granted US 5,663,484 to RiceTec concerning specified rice lines, plants, grains and breeding-related claims.

Indian institutions challenged claims that overlapped with characteristics of traditionally known Basmati rice. Evidence relating to existing varieties and grain characteristics was used in the dispute.

RiceTec subsequently withdrew several challenged claims, including claims 15–17, which concerned rice grains with characteristics similar to Basmati. This was a narrowing of the patent claims, not a cancellation of every claim in the entire patent.

The Basmati example also requires a distinction between patents and geographical indications. A patent concerns a qualifying invention; a geographical indication identifies goods whose characteristics or reputation are linked to a geographical origin. These forms of protection answer different questions.

Comparison of the 3 disputes

SubjectImportant patent factCentral issueOutcome
TurmericUS patent granted in 1995Already known wound-healing usePatent cancelled in 1997
NeemEuropean patent granted in 1994Earlier knowledge relevant to a neem-based fungicidal applicationPatent revoked in 2000
BasmatiRiceTec US patent granted in 1997Claims overlapping known rice characteristicsSeveral challenged claims withdrawn

What these cases establish

The successful challenge to a patent does not require the challenger's community to patent the traditional knowledge itself. Instead, reliable evidence of what was previously known may show that an applicant does not satisfy the requirements for a patent.

Equally, a dispute about an invalid patent does not answer every question about access to a biological resource, commercial benefit sharing or a geographical name. Those matters may be governed by separate legal mechanisms.

Prelims focus

  • Turmeric: US patent 5,401,504; granted 1995; cancelled 1997.
  • CSIR challenged the turmeric patent using evidence of prior knowledge.
  • Neem: European patent relating to a fungicidal application; revoked in 2000.
  • Basmati: RiceTec's US patent 5,663,484 was granted in 1997.
  • RiceTec withdrew several disputed Basmati-related claims, including claims 15–17.
  • Trap: The Basmati patent was not simply a patent on all Basmati rice, and its entire set of claims was not cancelled.

[CSIR-TKDL, 'Bio-piracy of Traditional Knowledge', Annex 1, entries 'Turmeric', 'Neem' and 'Basmati Rice', consulted 14 November 2026; NCERT, Biology, Class 12, chapter 12, section 12.4, 'Ethical Issues'; European Patent Office, neem patent opposition and appeal records relating to EP 0 436 257, consulted 14 November 2026.]

title: Landmark Biopiracy Disputes: Turmeric, Neem and Basmati Rice
